source_refs.note: Topic 3.5, printed pages 75-77: prokaryotic cell structure and the comparison table with eukaryotic cells. Figures 3.29 and 3.30 are carried by the Chapter 2 originals of the bacterial cell and the bacterial flagellum, with the axoneme figure of topic 3.4 for the eukaryotic side.

blocks.text: Bacteria and archaea are made of prokaryotic cells, whereas all other forms of life are composed of eukaryotic cells. Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have DNA as their genetic material; both have plasma membranes as their coverings; and both have ribosomes for protein synthesis. You have already gone through the details of the cell organelles.

Prokaryotic cells are much simpler than eukaryotic ones. Most prokaryotic cells are 2 to 8 µm long, about one tenth the size of a typical eukaryotic cell. A prokaryotic cell lacks a nucleus: its much less extensive DNA lies in a more or less central region known as the nucleoid (nucleus-like). A prokaryotic cell also lacks other membrane-bounded organelles such as the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, chloroplasts, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and peroxisomes. The entire cytoplasm is one unit with no internal support structures. Ribosomes are present but smaller than those of eukaryotic cells.

blocks.alt: A rod-shaped bacterium cut open lengthwise. From outside in: a dashed capsule, a thick cell wall, a thinner cell membrane, and cytoplasm with a tangled nucleoid of circular DNA, a small circular plasmid, scattered ribosomes and two mesosome infoldings of the membrane. A wavy flagellum extends from one end and short pili project from the surface.
blocks.caption: A generalised prokaryotic cell (original diagram, shared with Chapter 2, after Figure 3.29).
blocks.long_description: The prokaryotic cell has a capsule, a peptidoglycan cell wall and a plasma membrane. There is no nucleus: the circular DNA lies in the nucleoid, with extra small rings called plasmids. The 70S ribosomes are scattered freely in the cytoplasm; there are no membrane-bounded organelles. Pili are extensions for attachment and the flagellum, built of flagellin, is for movement.

blocks.text: The Svedberg values of the smaller and larger subunits of prokaryotic ribosomes are 30S and 50S, and the complete ribosome is 70S. Surrounding the plasma membrane of most prokaryotic cells is a cell wall, but it does not contain cellulose: it is composed of peptidoglycan, a single large polymer of amino acids and sugar. In bacteria the cell wall may be surrounded by a capsule and may have extensions for attachment known as pili (singular pilus). Prokaryotic flagella are made of repeating units of the protein flagellin and do not contain microtubule triplets. Mitosis and meiosis are missing in the prokaryotic cell; it divides by direct division (binary fission).

blocks.alt: A bacterial flagellum in side view: a basal body of rings set in the cell envelope layers, a curved hook, and a long helical filament extending outwards.
blocks.caption: A prokaryotic flagellum, built of flagellin with no microtubules (original diagram, shared with Chapter 2; compare with the 9 + 2 axoneme in topic 3.4, after Figure 3.30).
blocks.long_description: The prokaryotic flagellum is a rigid helical filament of the protein flagellin, joined by a hook to a basal body of rings that rotate in the cell envelope. It is not membrane-bounded and has no microtubules, unlike the eukaryotic flagellum, which is a membrane-covered axoneme of two central microtubules inside nine doublets.

blocks.caption: Difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
rows: One, but not a true chromosome; plasmids
Usually unicellular (some cyanobacteria may be multicellular)
Absent; chlorophyll scattered in the cytoplasm
No mitosis or meiosis; direct division (binary fission)
Membrane-bounded; two central microtubules in an outer ring of nine doublets
Not membrane-bounded; repeating units of flagellin; no microtubule triplets
Only in plant cells and fungi (chemically simpler)
Peptidoglycan, a single large polymer of amino acids and sugar

blocks.alt: Two panels. Prokaryote: a rod-shaped cell whose flagellum spins like a propeller; an inset shows the filament made of flagellin, a curved hook and a motor set in the cell wall and membrane, with no microtubules. Eukaryote: a cell whose flagellum beats in waves; an inset cross-section shows nine pairs of microtubules round two central ones (9 + 2), covered by the cell membrane.
